query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, controlled thermal aging at intermediate temperatures promotes the diffusion-driven formation of chemically enriched nanoclusters of Cr, Ni, and Mn at the grain boundaries. These nanoclusters reduce grain boundary cohesion and act as initiation sites for intergranular cracks under load, leading to brittle behavior that is distinct from conventional precipitation-driven embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, homogeneously distributed single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with uniform grain boundary composition.
generation.intervention: Subject one set of specimens to controlled thermal aging treatment (e.g., 350–450°C for selected durations under an inert atmosphere) designed to induce nanoclustering at grain boundaries without initiating secondary precipitate formation. The as-cast specimens serve as the control.
generation.conditions: Perform thermal aging under an inert (oxygen-free) atmosphere with durations carefully tuned to initiate nanoclustering. Follow with standardized tensile tests at room temperature and intermediate temperatures (e.g., 300–500°C) under both quasi-static and dynamic loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoclusters of Cr, Ni, and Mn forming along grain boundaries, as detected by atom probe tomography and confirmed by high-resolution TEM and energy dispersive spectroscopy. Additional XRD characterization will be used to verify the absence of secondary precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Unlike conventional alloys where embrittlement is often due to impurity segregation or coarse precipitate formation, in the HEA the thermal treatment induces subtle, diffusion-driven nanoclustering of the principal elements at the grain boundaries. These clusters lower the local grain boundary cohesion, making the GBs more susceptible to cracking under applied stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, thermally aged specimens will show a marked reduction in toughness, evidenced by earlier onset of intergranular cracking and brittle fracture during tensile tests. This reduction should be most pronounced at intermediate testing temperatures and under dynamic loading. Post-mortem analysis will reveal elemental enrichment (nanoclusters) at grain boundaries without evidence of secondary phase precipitation.
generation.baseline: As-cast specimens with uniform, unsegregated grain boundary composition, exhibiting higher toughness and predominantly ductile fracture behavior.
generation.boundary: The predicted brittle behavior will be observed only under the condition that the thermal aging parameters are within the range that promotes nanocluster formation without triggering secondary phase precipitation. At temperatures or aging times outside this regime (too low to initiate diffusion or too high/long enough to form precipitates), the mechanism and observed behavior may differ.
generation.uncertainty: While the supporting evidence strongly implies that nanoclustering drives the embrittlement in HEAs under these conditions, uncertainties remain regarding the precise kinetics of nanocluster formation and the potential emergence of incipient precipitates. Additional high-fidelity characterization is required to fully isolate the effect of nanoclusters from any other microstructural changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi HEA specimens: (A) as-cast control and (B) specimens aged at 350–450°C for varying durations. Incorporate routine checks using XRD and TEM to confirm the absence of any secondary precipitate formation in the aged samples. Conduct standardized tensile tests at both room and intermediate temperatures (300–500°C) under quasi-static and dynamic loading conditions.
measurements: Atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM to quantify and visualize nanocluster formation at the GBs.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses to rule out the presence of secondary precipitates.
Tensile test measurements of toughness, yield strength, and fracture patterns (e.g., intergranular vs. ductile dimple fracture).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged specimens that exhibit confirmed nanocluster formation do not show a statistically significant reduction in toughness compared to the as-cast control, or if secondary precipitates are detected that could account for embrittlement, then the hypothesis that nanoclustering alone drives brittle behavior will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

This indicates that the segregation of elements Cr, Ni, and Mn into GBs in current HEA occurred during tensile tests at 700°C. It has been shown that the residual strain generated by cold rolling can promote the diffusion of Cr into GBs during subsequent annealing processes, leading to the formation of Cr-rich σ phases in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs (, ). Therefore, it is reasonable to infer that plastic deformation can facilitate the segregation of elements Cr, Ni, and Mn into GBs in current HEA. However, the low-level concentration of these elements is insufficient for precipitating Cr-rich σ, body-centered cubic (bcc) Cr, or L10-NiMn phases (table S1) (, , ). In addition, the short exposure (10 min) at 700°C is insufficient to precipitate σ phase, as confirmed by TEM (Fig. 4A). S4 show that the C and B composition at Cr-enriched and Ni(Mn)-enriched GBs is very low, which is insufficient to form carbides or borides at GBs. A recent study of the single-phase fcc CoFeNi2V0.5Mo0.2 HEA demonstrated that the lack of Cr and Mn can evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (). Therefore, we believe that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs can embrittle GBs and, hence, lead to ductility loss with increasing deformation temperature. Note that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs also occurs at relatively low temperatures (<700°C), which accounts for ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. proposals.intervention: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens: (A) as-cast control with a homogeneous grain boundary composition and (B) specimens subjected to a controlled thermal aging treatment (e.g., 350–450°C for varying durations) to promote slow, diffusion-driven nanoclustering/segregation of elements (such as Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries.
proposals.conditions: Perform the thermal aging in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with aging durations tuned to just begin observable segregation. Follow with standardized tensile testing at both intermediate (e.g., 300–500°C) and room temperatures under quasi-static and dynamic loading conditions to mimic demanding service environments.
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoclustering of specific elements at the grain boundaries, as detected by atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM coupled with energy dispersive spectroscopy.
proposals.mechanism: In contrast to conventional alloys where brittleness is often due to precipitate formation or grain-boundary segregation from impurities, the hypothesis is that in a compositionally complex HEA, slow kinetic segregation leads to the formation of chemically enriched nanoclusters that reduce grain boundary cohesion. These localized changes initiate crack formation under stress, resulting in brittle behavior when the clustering reaches a critical threshold.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, thermally aged specimens will exhibit a marked reduction in toughness manifested by early intergranular fracture in tensile tests. This sensitivity should be more pronounced under dynamic loading and at intermediate temperatures. If brittleness emerges due to nanoclustering, measurements should reveal local chemical enrichment at the boundaries and correlated decohesion, differing from conventional precipitation-driven embrittlement.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This controlled comparison directly tests whether a physically distinct mechanism—elemental nanoclustering at grain boundaries driven by thermal activation in a homogeneous, single-phase HEA—is responsible for brittle behavior. It distinguishes the effects of chemical decohesion inherent to HEAs from conventional alloy mechanisms, thereby clarifying the origin of toughness degradation within these complex materials under service-like conditions.

critiques.addresses_problem: The direction directly targets the open question by testing whether nanoclustering of principal elements at grain boundaries in a single-phase HEA governs toughness loss, thereby distinguishing its mechanism from conventional alloys.
critiques.constraints: It respects the constraint by using a compositionally complex, single-phase CrMnFeCoNi alloy and retains its complexity while introducing controlled thermal aging to selectively promote elemental segregation under inert conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism—thermal activation driving nanoclustering of elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) that reduces grain boundary cohesion—is physically sound for HEAs, as similar effects have been observed and documented in the provided evidence.
critiques.feasibility: Preparation of as‐cast and thermally aged specimens; tensile testing at room/intermediate temperatures under quasi-static and dynamic conditions; and characterization by atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM are all feasible with established methods.
critiques.evidence: The proposed mechanism is well supported by prior work (e.g., PMC6897545 evidence entries indicate that nanoclustering and subsequent reduction in GB cohesion are correlated with ductility loss in HEAs).
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the thermal aging parameters might not exclusively induce nanoclustering without inadvertently initiating detectable secondary phase precipitation, which would complicate the interpretation of brittleness solely as a result of nanoclustering.
critiques.fix: Include additional characterization (e.g., XRD or complementary TEM analyses) at each aging duration to ensure that no secondary precipitates form, isolating the nanoclustering effect as the source of embrittlement.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly targets the open question by testing whether nanoclustering of principal elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries in an initially single-phase CrMnFeCoNi HEA leads to a loss of toughness, a mechanism distinct from conventional alloy embrittlement. Although there is a risk that the thermal aging might trigger secondary precipitates that could confound the interpretation, this risk is manageable by adding supplementary characterization (e.g., XRD or additional high-resolution TEM analyses) at each aging duration. The supporting evidence from multiple PMC6897545 records strongly backs up the proposed mechanism, making direction A the optimal choice with the suggested fix.
